content.text: Agents refer to AI systems that can act autonomously to achieve goals, often using tools and reasoning. AI agents are powered by a large language model (LLM) and an agent harness, which allows the agent to interact with tools, APIs, and other systems. Agents can be used for a variety of tasks, including research, coding, and more.

content.text: Agents can use tools to interact with their environment and other systems, enabling them to perform complex tasks. While a large language model (LLM) can reason over and produce text, it can't interact with external tools, APIs, or systems on its own. When we provide tools to an agent it allows the agent to take actions in the environment and pull in information that wasn't in the LLM's training data.

content.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have a limited context window, which is the amount of input (commonly text) that it can process at one time to complete a task (Stanford AI). Given this constraint, when an LLM is wrapped in an agent harness, one of its tasks is managing this context. The important piece to understand is that the limitation on the context an agent can work with at any one time makes managing context critical. There are many approaches to this including just dropping older context and summarizing the current context using an LLM. The resources below dive deeper into how context management works in real agents.

content.text: Tokens are small pieces of text that make up an AI model's context. Models process text as tokens rather than whole words, and token counts show how much context is being used.

content.text: An agent harness is a framework or environment that allows an AI agent to interact with tools, APIs, and other systems. It provides the necessary infrastructure for the agent to perform tasks, manage context, and make decisions effectively.

content.caption: A harness wraps around a model to create an agent. Simply model + harness = agent.
